utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness seeks limited protection as set out at the foot of the second page of the draft summary, and, indeed, as separately applied for. He seeks face distortion and pseudonym. He does so on the ground that he returns to the place of which he will be speaking on a regular basis for work, more significantly is planning to move back to his former house with his family. His concerns are, I accept, of the conventional type, and I don't have any particular matters to draw to your attention beyond the fact that he is returning to his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kordic has nothing against these protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will make the order as asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The only exhibit to which this witness will be referring is the town map of Zepce, 2284, which I'll ask to be placed on the ELMO. I don't think the witness is, in fact, particularly adept at dealing with maps, but I think that it will be useful for pointing out some general features.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for the next witness will be Witness AH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delay. The former witness room for this court has now been allocated to a member of the judiciary, and so the witness room for this court is now the same as the witness room for the small court, and it may be taking the usher a little longer to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have been granted protection by the Judges of this Court and will, for the purposes of your evidence, be known as Witness AH. Will you please look at the piece of paper that the usher will give you. Don't read out the name on the piece of paper, but simply say yes if that is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness AH, were you born in Zenica in 1972, but lived your life thereafter, until the war, in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have on the ELMO the map 2284. It may be better, actually, if the witness has the one -- is that one black and white or does it have blue on it? I'll hand mine in because mine has actually got blue on it which helps with the identification of the river. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The part of Zepce in which you lived was called what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Zenicki Put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the map, noticing, for example, where the railway line crosses the map and where the railway station can be seen, can you give a rough indication, using the pointer, where Zenicki Put is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Close to the railway station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you join the Territorial Defence at the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many members of the Territorial Defence were usually on duty during the war, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How well-armed or otherwise were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Poorly. They weren't well-armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What duties did the Territorial Defence undertake in the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Mostly they held the points around the town, access points to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the attack of the 24th of June, were Croat families who had lived in Zenicki Put noted to be moving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were they moving to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Mostly where there was a Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any one particular part of the town that was noted for being Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: There was a part of town, it was called Varosiste, in the upper part of town, and that's where the Croats mostly went, to their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point that to us on the map. We can see something called Vasariste, which is rather similar but may be different. Where is Varosiste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Varosiste is next to the road but a little further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long before the 24th of June, approximately, were you aware of Croats moving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The night before, the night before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th of June, at what time were you first aware of shooting or fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: In the morning, at 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From which direction did the shooting come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: It came from the direction of Papratnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able, on the map, to point out that place or the direction of that place, please? We can't see it at the moment on the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: You can't see it on the screen, but it's above Ljubna. Papratnica is above Ljubna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that is therefore to the west of the town of Zepce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the resident Muslims of Zenicki Put decide to attempt to defend their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, they did, they defended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time in the morning, were you on or off duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon in your possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in turn, did the HVO have troops at one or more than one location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: More than one location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please list them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The old post office, which isn't shown on the map but it is below the railway station, below the railway station, and the members of the military police of the HVO were located there. The building of the Balkan Hotel, once again this is not shown on the map, but they were located -- that is to say, the HVO army was located in that building as well. The members of the Andrija Tadic Battalion were located in Tatat Budzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Tatar Budzak is where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Here it is, here on the map [indicates]. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you. The old post office, as we can see, is comparatively close to Zenicki Put. To your knowledge, roughly how many members of the military police were there, and by whom were they commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I don't know. About 20 of them. The commander, their commander, was -- he is a native of Teslic, Luka Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your home, were you able to see something of what was going on in detail, and in particular were you able to see something of the family of Osman Tukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them being taken out and taken off to the Lovacki Dom or hunting lodge, which is where the military prison of the HVO was located, and they were taken off in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many were there in the family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Four family members of the Tukic family and three of the Kahriman family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the Tukic family was man, wife, and two sons, and Amir and Edin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: And two children. Edin, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have any of those seven people been seen since?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did the fighting in Zepce that started on the 24th of June last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: In the old part of town, it lasted for about seven days, whereas the settlement across from that, it went on for about three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the old part of town, who won, and when was there a surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The HVO won in the centre of town, and there was a surrender, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the date of the surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were people killed in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which was the last area to give up resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The Zenicki Put area, so that they took settlement by settlement and what was left was Zenicki Put, and the people had stationed themselves there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were a number of Muslims captured at that stage and taken into detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: One hundred and five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they taken to a series of places, and if so, can you just give us the series without necessarily finding them all on the map? Where were they taken first and where subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: First they were taken to the silos. The silo isn't on the map, I can't see it on the map. After that, they were taken from the silos to the hangars of the Nova Trgovina, which is on the map, the new shop, and the women and children were put up there. When they saw that there was no room to take us in, they transferred us to the PT hall of the primary school, which is located in this area here [indicates]. But that wasn't a gymnastics hall, it was just a room, six by seven metres, where they put 105 people in for seven days without food, without water, without anything, without any facilities at all; no toilet facilities, nothing of that kind, just an ordinary room. And later they released us; that is to say, seven days later, when it had been raining intensely, they took us outside to drink some water, and we did what we could on this polygon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What quantity of water was made available for the 105 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: After five days, they gave us five litres of water for the 105 individuals that were held there. They gave us a canister of water. And then seven days later, they let us go out, and people just drank water from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did this period of detention for you end or change? Where did you go from the gymnasium or from the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: We were transported to the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how long were you detained in the silo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I stayed there until the end of my detention, until I escaped from the camp, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which was on what day or what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: It was the 20th of November, 1993, up until that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your detention in the silos was in what accommodation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: They were cells, and the grain was loaded there from the Nova Trgovina, and there would be 60 people to a cell. We slept on wooden pallets. There were no toilet facilities or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many cells altogether were occupied, apart from the cell in which you were staying and detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Ten cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how many prisoners there were kept in the other cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: On an average, 60 to a cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How big was each cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Perhaps about eight metres long and four metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During the detention at the silos, were those detained taken to do any work for those who were detaining them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What work and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: All kinds of work; digging trenches every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts, if you can list the places, were people taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: To the front lines, Blagojevica Brdo, which isn't on the map, Devila, Zovik, Varda, Kremen, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will find those at paragraph 13 rather than at paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of these forced labours, were prisoners injured or killed, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how many prisoners, approximately, were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, on an average, about a hundred people were killed, perhaps more. About a hundred, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For what period of detention were you forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Throughout the time I was there, five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose trenches were you digging, whose positions were you digging trenches for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Both for the HVO and for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain how it came about that you were digging trenches for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Well, I don't know exactly, but I think it was sometime in July that the Serbs came with trucks, 110-type trucks, military ones. They loaded us up 20 to a truck under the awning. We didn't see where we were going, and the journey took three hours. We came to a place -- when we crossed the Bosna River, the pontoon bridge -- between Maglaj and Zavidovici, there was a pontoon bridge erected and we crossed that, and we saw -- they took the tarpaulin off, and we saw that it was the Serbs who were taking us somewhere. We continued our journey by truck towards Ozren, and that's where we started digging above the Serb positions. I was there for about 20 days with no facilities whatsoever. We slept in some kind of garage. It was a room three-by-five metres, and we spent 20 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the trenches you were digging were for the Serbs at a front line between the Serbs and whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Between the BH army, towards Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were made available to the Serbs by your captors, was there any suggestion that they were being compelled to make you available, or did it appear that this was happening by consent and agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: By agreement, yes. Everything was done by agreement with the Serbs, the fall of Zepce and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you'd finished your trench-digging for the Serbs, where did you go? By whom were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The Serbs took us back again to the HVO police, who then took us over and took us then back again to the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your detention, were you aware of prisoners being taken to Novi Seher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you one of those prisoners or was this something you learned of from others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened at Novi Seher?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: They took us there to work, to loot houses, bring things out. We also demolished some houses which were in their way, and they were taking away whatever they could lay their hands on. Plundered everything, set fire to things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What ethnic community, if there was an ethnicity to the community, had Novi Seher been?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The centre of the town was mostly Muslim, and Croats lived around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know whose houses you were being instructed to loot? What ethnicity were the owners of the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your detention in the silos, was there something that happened to somebody called Jasmin, whose name you may not know in full but whose position you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Jasmin, yes. I don't know his last name. Yes, it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was he? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: He was a member of a military unit in Zepce, I don't know what that was called, and what came to pass to him, well, they took him out in the evening, around 12, from cell number 6. He was called out, "Jasmin, come out," and he did. I could not see because it was nighttime, and the cells were such that you couldn't really see anyone. They were very tall; there were no windows or anything. They were beating him, we could hear that, until he fell down, I believe, and subsequently he succumbed to that battering, because they beat him all that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the only example of maltreatment at night, or was there other evidence to suggest people being dealt with at night in the silos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, that was not the only such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What other examples can you give us of things heard or seen at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Similarly, they would come in the evening hours, call out, beat with whatever they could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an occasion before your release when you were at the Previla front line, and when you saw something happening --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Previla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and you saw somebody happening to somebody called Senaid Mujetekic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Mujetekic, Senaid Mujetekic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I can, yes. We were digging trenches there. There were three of us, and two of us were sent to go down to the village, which was a little lower, to bring some boards, wooden boards for the trenches, and when we came back, he was lying there dead. The HVO soldiers said that he was about to flee, and that was how he was shot. He was hit in the back and the exit wound was in his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, this front line was the front line between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The HVO and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were taken trench-digging, what sort of food, if any, were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: We were, but it was of very poor quality. Two meals at times, but very poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of liquid were you provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In plentiful supply or limited? Explain, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, at times, it was adequate; at times, it wasn't. It depended on the site that you were sent to work at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What percentage, if you can help us, of the time of your detention between July and, I think, November of 1993 were you forced to work for your captors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Throughout, all those five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When people died in the course of trench-digging, can you explain, in general terms, how it was that they died? What was the circumstances of their being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, mostly along the front line, as they were digging trenches. Naturally, because you are in front of the front line, you're digging a trench, and you simply get killed, and then they say, "Well, it's your own folk who killed you."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While people were digging trenches, exposed to the people on the other side, where were the captors and how exposed were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. While you were digging trenches, exposed to the risk of being killed, where were the captors, the people who brought you there, either the HVO or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: They were behind us, behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they better protected than you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Of course they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You saw something of some graves in the Zepce cemetery. Tell us about that, please. Paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that, and were you, indeed, involved in some of the acts of burial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, I also participated in the burial of people who had been killed at the front lines. Some were taken to the cemetery and some were buried -- or, rather, simply covered with some earth on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one man, indeed, killed working beside you in Pazaric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see his burial or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: He was buried right there, in Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, no. At Pazaric, near Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to Zepce, how many graves did you see or count in Zepce that related to people killed at the front lines trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Around 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness AH, allow me to introduce myself. I'm Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I'm one of the Defence team for Mr. Dario Kordic. I will now ask you a few questions. However, before we begin, the routine remark, will you please pause before you answer, after you've heard my question, so as to give the interpreters time to interpret. Witness AH, if I understood you properly, you were a member of the Territorial Defence, sometime since April or May 1992; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you stayed with the Territorial Defence even after the 319th Mountain Brigade of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was it the regular defence in the town of Zepce? Because if I understand properly, it had three companies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You made a statement to the investigators on the 27th of July, 1996, and then you said that after the 319th Mountain Brigade was founded, the Territorial Defence in Zepce was left with three companies, "and I was a member of one of them."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Three companies were not in the town itself, they were on the front lines against the Serbs. In the town itself, there were only two units, each 50 men strong, and they were simply guarding individual facilities, checkpoints. But in the town, there were no three companies there because the Zepce municipality is not only a town. You know what a municipality is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. So of those three TO companies, a company of some 100 strong was stationed in the town itself, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, will you agree with me that in addition to this one TO company, in the town of Zepce was also the headquarters of the so-called Green Berets. We might describe it as a special unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Like Andrija Tadic's, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, I should say, a special unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: You mean like the one of Andrija Tadic's?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I am asking that question, Witness AH. Will you agree with me that in the town of Zepce, a Green Beret unit was stationed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, but they were under the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But will you agree with me that their headquarters was in the pensioners' home in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the command of the Territorial Defence was first in the secondary school and then moved over to the silo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, not to the silo, next to the silo, sir. That was the seat of Nova Trgovina, and that is where their headquarters were. The silo was kept by the HVO because it was from the silo that the command of the BH army was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. But we agree that they were next door.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, they were next-door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the town, apart from the Green Berets, were there any special task forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness AH, as a member of a TO company, you were deployed in the town, you did not leave the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Most of the time while you were a member of the TO, you manned the checkpoint at the entry to a town called Carsija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Called na petlji, yes. It was right at the entry into the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That was a checkpoint manned by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Three members of the army were killed by the HVO at that checkpoint -- no, two; one was wounded -- because they were bothered by that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you allow me to ask you my questions, and then the Prosecution can later on ask you some more questions. We shall agree that this checkpoint was manned by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness AH, will you agree with me that in the town, and one might say in the municipality of Zepce, the mistrust between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina began to mount after the conflict broke out between the Croat and Muslim population in the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: It could be, because the Croat rear was protected by the Serbs. They were joined with us, allied with us, and yet they were in collusion with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that the provocation was not one-sided, that Muslim forces were also provoking Croat forces in the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, yes, some might say that there were provocations on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I meant, in the first place, the provocations caused in the town by the members of the Green Berets from time to time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Could be, but I wasn't a member of that unit so I wouldn't really know, would I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you must have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, we've all heard this or that rumour, that is quite true. I mean, everybody knew about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So we shall agree in principle, to round off this subject, that in principle, in the town of Zepce, there were two armies, if I may put it that way, with two separate commands.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Well, they were not really separate because there was cooperation between the army of BH and the HVO until shooting started. They cooperated, but a third party was also involved in this matter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness AH, that particular day, the 24th of June, is the day of Sir John the Baptist, and Catholics always mark it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Sir, do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No. Will you please answer this: Are you aware of that Catholic holiday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I am. But may I tell you something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, you may not. Will you please just answer my questions, just let me ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with this in an orderly way. What's the relevance of the holiday, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already discussed it once. I merely wanted to see whether the witness was aware whether the Croat Catholics, not only Croat Catholics but all Catholics, whether they mark that particular day, whether this is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to know what the relevance of this is. That's the question. Why are you asking this question? What's the point of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an introduction to my second question, who launched the attack on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of the question whether it's a holiday or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honour, the Croats could not have launched an attack on that day; they were attacked. They were getting ready for the holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They were on holiday and they didn't launch the attack; that's the point, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not launch an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll put that to the witness. Just don't interrupt. Witness AH, you've heard it suggested that the Croats were on holiday that day and didn't launch the attack; is that true or not? You can deal with it briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No. No, that is not true. I don't know about the holiday, but they were getting ready, the Croats were getting ready for that day. Perhaps they were not planning to attack on that particular day, but it turned out that they did. They were digging trenches in the town before the conflict, they were already building up their defenses, and whatever facility they held, it was surrounded by trenches. I mean, there is no doubt about that. Perhaps he knows because they attacked on that day. Perhaps they should have attacked on a Friday, when our people go to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness AH, do you know anything, and will you agree with me that on the 24th of June, 1993, that situation that we talked about culminated; that is, a subversive group of the BH army entered the area of Gornji Papratnica, in the area of Krnak, and killed two HVO soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was at home at the time. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps -- and if you don't, of course, that is an answer too -- what happened in Begov Han on that same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, I don't, because I wasn't up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Today you talked about how you had organized your defence, and if I understood you properly, in defending your part of town, it was you, members of your company, who participated, those who were on duty; that is, some 50 of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I was at home at the time. I got up at around 9, and then I heard the gunfire. So evidently I had to defend my home. I couldn't leave it, I couldn't leave my home. I never went to attack your home. I was standing by my home. Sir, I had no weapons or anything. What could I defend it with; a shovel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. But you will agree with me -- I'm sure you will agree with me that the fighting went on for almost a whole week, I mean fighting between the HVO and the army of BH, for seven days in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: But it went on for over three months across the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So since you were fighting for seven days, one might infer from that that, militarily speaking, you were not inferior, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No. I was at home, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the majority of houses in Zepce were damaged during that week of fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes, and three mosques were destroyed and put fire to, and I believe there is evidence to that effect in -- as a matter of fact, four of them, four, during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, will you agree with me that those 105 men who were with you, were they all able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No. There were also civilians over 60 years old and elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions, Your Honours. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About four questions arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The four mosques that were destroyed, do you know if, in the course of the fighting, they were used by your side as military installations? Do you know how they were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: I think that mosques are not military installations. We know what mosques are for; for prayers, like any other religious buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how they were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: The one in town was set on fire, the one up there near Trzanska, or was mined and ruined to the ground. Just the walls are left standing. The other one in Prijeko, that too was destroyed. Now it has been repaired. And there is another small one in Mahala, an old wooden mosque. That too was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you that your side started the fighting. Was there any truth in that, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. I know that we were together with the HVO. Until the very conflict itself, we were allies, until the 24th. With our neighbours, we cooperated normally. Everything was fine. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When your neighbours left the area in which you lived on the day before, was there any explanation given by them for why they were doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't explain anything. We just saw them going, taking things out. That was a sufficient indication that something was in the offing, but we didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the course of the time when you were taken out by the HVO to go trench-digging, was it ever suggested to you that you were in some way the authors of your own misfortune because you had started this attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: No, no one said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, you said that the checkpoint at Naputa, on the outside of the town, was of particular importance and it bothered them. Can you just explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: They wanted it removed probably because -- I don't know. We held that checkpoint because two or three months before the conflict, two of our members were killed at night. They were on duty, and they were killed. I don't really know how. Anyway, it was at night with a hand-held rocket launcher. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's why I ask. But I note that the trench-digging itself and the circumstances hasn't been challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AH, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one further witness for this week whom Mr. Scott is dealing with at the moment. I'm not sure whether the witness is yet ready to start giving evidence. If not, then we can perhaps deal with some of the administrative matters, but each of those would also benefit from the attendance of Mr. Scott, and he can always complete dealing with the witness in a break, if the witness isn't ready now. I've asked Mr. Scott to come, and I hope he'll be here imminently, if you'll indulge me with just a few minutes until he does. I can tell the Chamber, while waiting, that the position for next week and the witnesses is as gloomy as I forecast, subject, of course, to any subpoenas being answered. The position is that there is one witness, I think, who is going to attend. I'm just trying to find the name. But it seems to me possible, with cooperation, that we could take the issue of Mr. Elford and his map next week, and rather than simply go into the matter in the absence of the witness, the proper course might be for him to come to explain who he is and what he's done, in general terms, and then such arguments as may follow can be addressed. There's also the witness Spork, an investigator, who I think will be available next week, possibly more for Tuesday than Monday, who can give evidence in relation to the Viteska Brigade exhibits, in particular. By bringing those two witnesses up the list, we will make better use of next week and may free up the following week for any other witnesses who, it may be, have to be called as a result of applications made and discussed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Looking at the latest list, I think, in front of us, the 4th of February, two of the witnesses for next week have been called. The last witness for this week, I take it, is about to come, and he is number 8 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may be now looking at a different list from Your Honour. I'm sorry about that. I'll see if I can find the right list. I'm not sure that I have that list with me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. But I've got a list here. Two of whom are said to be subject to subpoena. One was sick and unwilling. Another one was unwilling, and only two remain there. Have you, in fact, got any other witnesses besides those that you've mentioned to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For next week, no, we've only got the one at the moment. On the list, it's number 4 and the initials are M.D., but they may be differently numbered. We don't, of course, know what is going to be the response of witnesses to the latest subpoenas issued by the Court. We can be hopeful, but we can't necessarily be optimistic. We've made every inquiry to try and advance the dates of the witnesses of the week of the 28th, and they are apparently all immovable, although we're having a last try at one of them, number 2, to see if he can come earlier, but so far the news is not encouraging. For that week, the week of the 28th, witness number 3, at least on the list I have, which is initials A.H., has now been discovered to have particular problems. The witness lives in another country. We've been notified very recently that he has no travel document and is of a status that makes the obtaining of a travel document for a short period of time virtually impossible. Again, that matter is being pursued vigorously. We've only just been informed of the travel difficulties that that witness may face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have an up-to-date list when you can produce it, because clearly I haven't got this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'll get Ms. Bower to print off the up-to-date list this morning, and then we can all speak from the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter it may be that we can attend to next week is this: that we, the Trial Chamber, would find it helpful in the case of the transcript witnesses -- I was going to deal with this when we came to it -- to know the passages in the transcript upon which the parties rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that exercise will take a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can possibly go through it next week, both sides pointing out what it is they say is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's one exercise that would be very usefully done next week, and there's another that I think can be done next week, which is to deal with the outstanding exhibits. There has been a comprehensive reply given, indicating what are objected to and on what grounds, and Mr. Lopez-Terres is leading the work responding to that, but there are bound to be some outstanding issues. Dependent on the resolution of those issues, then there will be a witness to be called to deal with production of exhibits to ask them, through us, to the Court. But the first exercise is to see what's properly challenged and what can be dealt with by way of agreement. Probably quite a lengthy exercise, first between the parties and second involving the Court, but no way around it, if the Court is to have the library of documents that we want it to have. I'm sorry that Mr. Scott doesn't appear, as I had rather hoped he would have done. It would be very early to take the break now, I realize. It would be very early to take the break now. We could, if this wasn't too inconvenient to the staff, take my ex parte, which is mostly a matter of notification of developments to the Court and, to some degree, a request for action, we could possibly take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Unless there are any matters the Defence want to raise, that would seem a sensible way of dealing with things. We'll take the ex parte and then we'll take the break. So half past 11.00, at the earliest, we'll sit again. If some other time, we'll notify you. I think we've all got to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will rise and we will reconvene in ex parte session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 10.38 a.m. for an Ex Parte Hearing 5 6 7 8 9 10 11

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the transcripts, I think the last document that we all shared was the 24-page document which had been, I think, initially prepared by Mr. Scott and then made available in electronic form for the Defence to put their comments on. I think that's right. I think the Chamber was going to see if it could find the time to look at that, rather than for us going through them slavishly one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's going to be possible to do it without going through the point -- I just make the few general points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first is this: that of course the Tulica decision dealt partly with transcripts, and summarizing the finding, the holding, it was that witnesses who had given evidence in this trial, their transcripts could not be admitted. The transcripts of those who have not given evidence was held admissible, subject to a Defence application to cross-examine on the ground that significant relevant matter wasn't covered by the cross-examination in Blaskic. So that, no doubt, is the test that we would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a -- looking at the Defence document, which may be a convenient one to start with, there are references in some cases to evidence being duplicative our cumulative. That, of course, is a matter for the Trial Chamber, to determine what is cumulative and what isn't, and what is therefore unnecessary. There are also points about admissibility which, speaking for myself, I think it very often goes more to questions of weight, as we have been tending to rule here; objections on hearsay grounds, that sort of thing. I must say some evidence does seem to be cumulative, and in some cases there is evidence directly about the accused. And again speaking for myself, it may be that those are witnesses who may have to be called in due course if they give direct prejudicial evidence. But having said that, what course are you inviting us to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, I think Your Honour has pretty well identified the general topics that are covered by the objections. There are one or two other specific requirements by the Defence for documents that may have been available to the witnesses when they were giving evidence but aren't available to the Prosecution now, for one reason or another; diaries and cables and so on. There are a couple of occasions where it seems to be said that witnesses lied in evidence. I haven't yet been able to go through all of those chapter and verse, but the answer to that is, of course, that if the lies revealed on the document itself in the transcript, why, then that goes to questions of weight. There is a reference to two other general topics as a ground for exclusion; one, the elaboration of Kordic's role and, second, the absence at the time of the transcribed evidence of further milinfosums that are now available. But, of course, if they are now available and have, indeed, been produced in evidence, then their value has already been placed before the Chamber and it's hard to see why it's necessary for them to be gone through with other witnesses beyond the witnesses with whom they've already been explored. So it's our respectful submission that there are no particular -- there is no particular strong objection to be found in any of the generic objections that are raised, and it may be that, indeed, it would be appropriate to go through them, however unhappy an exercise in one way, one by one where any objection is stated. Before I invite the Court, subject to any observations by my friends opposite, before I invite the Court to do that, we have in mind what His Honour -- Your Honour, I think, said first thing this morning about selecting the relevant pages to be read. That will be a fairly extensive exercise, but of course it will be done. I think our expectation was, in any event, for transcribed witnesses, that where they were going to be admitted in general terms, they would be admitted but the Chamber wouldn't be expected to sit down and slavishly read them because the evidence would be there for consideration and the parties could draw on whatever passages they wanted in argument, bearing in mind that each party effectively has the right to comment on the other side's selection in the process of written and verbal arguments made either at half-time or at the end of the case. But, of course, that exercise will be gone through at some stage, and if the Chamber requires it to be done immediately or next week, then it could certainly be done as soon as may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful to have the passages relied on. I'm not suggesting they be read out but simply that reference is made to them --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- so that we know what the parties say about a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That may be somewhat difficult particularly with, say, village witnesses, where their whole evidence is a narrative account, but we will, of course, do whatever we can. I suppose there's one other general point to be made. The question of whether selected passages can be relied upon is something that has occurred in relation to Blaskic and his evidence, and on that we see that the Defence says, at page 24, last entry, "Nothing prohibits the Prosecution from calling this witness live." Not, of course, something we are likely to do, given the probable similarity or identity of interests of the defendants in certain or many areas. However, if we only wish the witness's transcript in relation to, for example, the phone calls that he acknowledges making and about which he was capable of being cross-examined, and if it's only those passages but all of them that go in, then the question of calling the witness lies simply shouldn't arise unless, on that narrow topic, there is genuinely some additional cross-examination beyond the cross-examination already conducted that should be made and could be identified. So, in short, General Blaskic falls into the same category of any other witness, notwithstanding his particular status, subject to the fact that, of course, he's not a witness who we would want to call live and expose to general cross-examination. That would be quite inappropriate. Having said that, I don't know if it would be helpful and realistic to see how many we can get through to seek the judgement of the Court on outstanding objections. It's seemed to us, with respect and in light of the Tulica decision, that the onus is substantially on the Defence to justify, by reason of identification of additional cross-examination, why witnesses cannot be taken as read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything the Defence want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one general matter for the record, Your Honour. We are concerned about the impact of wholesale import of testimony from other cases into this case and its adverse impact upon the public trial, if you like, given that about 40 per cent of the witnesses have sought, in some form or another, protective measures, and I do not think that we have necessarily objected to that. But I have to say that I do have a lot of concern about the wholesale importation of about 48 transcripts, which by our count, anyway, amount to some 12,300 pages of testimony, from witnesses that the Trial Chamber will never have the opportunity to see, whom our client will never have the opportunity to confront, and whose credibility, obviously, the Trial Chamber will have no opportunity at all to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the opportunity of reading the transcript and assessing -- from the cross-examination or the examination, it can make an assessment of credibility. What we won't have done, of course, is to have seen the demeanour of the witness. But that apart, it could make an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Quite so, Your Honour. I readily acknowledge that. But there is a certain advantage to seeing the manner of delivery. That doesn't require any elaboration on my part. You're professional judges. You well know the advantage of that. The second point that I would like to make, and I won't reiterate it, is the arguments I've already made regarding the Aleksovski case, the unusual circumstances that were presented in that case, the indisputable probative value that the evidence was found to have, and the procedural stage at which the application was made in that case. I've already made all those points, and there's no point in repeating them. Insofar as two small matters that the Prosecution raised are concerned, one deals with matters available to counsel in prior cases but not available to us; for example, diplomatic cables regarding one witness, a diary that was used in redirect examination from another witness, Mr. Ashdown, which we have requested. It's not been provided to us. We've requested the diplomatic cables. They've not been provided to us. It seems peculiar, to use a fairly understated term, that material that was available to the Defence which actually cross-examined the witness is not available to us in order for us to be able to determine whether an effective job of cross-examination was done. And so insofar as those witnesses are concerned, there is an objection, and I think it's a well-taken one. Finally, with respect to General Blaskic's testimony, I do not think that there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He may be in a separate category. We'll have to have argument on that when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as my colleague Kovacic is responsible for addressing this problem and unfortunately he's not today in the courtroom because we did not think that it would be on the agenda, I can only more or less repeat or say something along the lines of Mr. Sayers' statement. If we remember how much transcripts from other cases were used in the Aleksovski case, then we can indeed see that those were some outstanding circumstances, that is, things that were really far from ordinary. Here we hear that the Prosecution is proposing to produce 48 transcripts. We heard our 93rd witness today, and that seems to indicate, at first glance already, that here we're not dealing with the same circumstances as in the Aleksovski case, so that, in principle, we do not think that it can be something that would make Mr. Cerkez' Defence very happy. However, of course, certain circumstances may be agreed upon, but we are dealing here with details, and I believe that that will be -- the discussion about that is scheduled for next week and Mr. Kovacic will be back here, so he will be able to tackle the issue. At the moment, he is precisely very busy studying all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is unsatisfactory, because it was made plain that we were going to discuss these transcripts at a fairly early date, as I recollect, and it's unsatisfactory that he is not here to deal with it. Is he in The Hague or is he elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic is in his office here, and he could be here in 15 minutes' time. So if you so decide, he can be here in the afternoon and say what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think the position is you're not ready with your witness, are you, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, almost but not quite.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make one suggestion that might help. Of course, there is a number of these witnesses who have no bearing on Mr. Cerkez at all; for instance, witnesses from Kiseljak would have absolutely no bearing on the case against Mr. Cerkez, or Vares, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are some cases where he apparently has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we could look at those. Let's try and get some, at least, out of the way. The witnesses where there are no objections, as I understand it, are 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 16, I think, may come next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 22, I beg your pardon, and 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I also, reading the document, found that there were other areas where there was apparently no objection. That was on behalf of Mr. Kordic. Number 25, 29, 34, and 39. What we could do is this: We can deal with some of the matters on which apparently there is no objection on behalf of Mr. Cerkez, and, Mr. Mikulicic, would you please have Mr. Kovacic here at 2.30 so that we can go through the -- or soon thereafter so that we can have his input into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other point to make. I entirely agree with Mr. Sayers that we must not overlook the needs for a public hearing so far as possible. The Court made reference to that this morning. I'm sure that once transcripts are -- it's decided what transcripts are in, a summary of the material can be read in to the record quite shortly, if that would be appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and, of course, arguments and judgements, insofar as they rely on witnesses, can, subject to measures of protection, give chapter and verse. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the position is unsatisfactory. We will do what we can without Mr. Kovacic. I mentioned, and Judge Bennouna mentions to me that it may be sensible to look at this matter from the point of view of categories. I've mentioned various categories.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not on-air. I've mentioned various categories, and Judge Bennouna points out that it may be helpful to look at some of these transcripts in terms of categories. We'd be sensible to look, at least to start with, at some of those where it appears that Mr. Cerkez has no objection, but on behalf of Mr. Kordic there is an objection. I have in mind number 3, Mr. Ashdown, who gives evidence about a conversation with Dr. Tudjman. The objection is, apparently, that it was a conversation when drink had been taken at a dinner. I recollect at the time that the evidence was given that it got some publicity, and there was extensive cross-examination on precisely this point, as to how much they'd had to drink. Now, what weight we give to it is a matter for us, but the matter was covered in cross-examination. And then there's a reference to a diary. Again, that's a matter for weight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I can articulate Mr. Kordic's position. Actually, it should be a conditional objection. The only thing that we wanted to see was what was produced to Defence counsel in the Blaskic case, and it may well be that upon review of the diary, Your Honour, the objection would be withdrawn. But we felt that we had to make the objection, since some material was available to Defence counsel in the Blaskic case which has not been made available to us, and that's really the position, simply stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is the diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The diary wasn't made an exhibit. We've made every effort to see if we can find a copy of it here in the building. We've not been able to do that. If the diary has any particular significance, no doubt it will have been referred to in argument in Blaskic and/or will appear in the judgement, if it's got any significance. We will continue to try and find a copy of the diary, if one exists here. We've, indeed, I think, asked assistance already through one of the ministries in London. If it's produced, it can be made available, and we would, of course, have no objection to any reliance by the Defence on what may emerge in any judgement in Blaskic in relation to this topic. While I'm on my feet, and I think Mr. Scott and I will deal with them some and some, can I respectfully invite the Chamber to consider this as the solution or a solution to the public hearing point: If and when the Chamber decides that a transcript is to be taken in evidence, it may be that the existing short summary on the left-hand side could simply be read, because we're in public session, to identify the witness and the general topic covered, and if the summary given there isn't sufficient, then a further summary could be read, but it may well be in most cases that that summary would take care of the problem. It would let the public know the general category of material being relied upon, subject to chapter and verse being spoken of later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Four is the next one, the inhabitant of Gomionica. The objection appears to be that he gave inconsistent testimony and that he testified to a sniper attack without any personal knowledge. Again, at first blush, it appears to me that those are matters entirely within the Trial Chamber's ability to deal with. A point was obviously made in the transcript, and it's a matter for argument. But I'll hear what anybody says about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do not have any further argument, Your Honour. I think it's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Number 5, there's no objection. Number 6, there's no objection. Number 7, again, no objection on behalf of Mr. Cerkez. This is a witness from Rotilj. Again, the objection is that the testimony is inconsistent, and a point is made about the timing of some words which were seen written. Again, is there anything to be added to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just the point under the basis for the objection, Your Honour, and that is that not all of the exhibits referred to in the transcript have been provided to Defence counsel in this case. It seems to me that just in view of fundamental fairness, in order to be able to evaluate the whole impact of the testimony, we should be entitled to see the exhibits. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the Prosecution's position with regard to the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not -- I have to say that, in fairness, I have not looked at those two exhibits that are referenced here, if I understand well, D122 and D123, which were apparently Defence Exhibits. As a matter of principle, I wouldn't think we would have a general objection with those being disclosed, subject to whatever protections they may have been given from the earlier case and again, Your Honour, with the proviso that I have not specifically seen them recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I notice that the same point may be made in relation to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, 372, I suppose. Again, I have no reason to object to that. I'm sure that that was apparently a Prosecution exhibit, and there again, Your Honour, I have no reason to think that we would have reason not to disclose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Anything further you want to say about number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 9, I understand, is no longer relied on. Number 10, now, this is one of the witnesses who does give direct evidence about Mr. Kordic; speaks of close contact between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic and other individuals, as well as the special purpose units. It's pointed out there's no objection from Mr. Kordic but there is an objection in relation to Mr. Cerkez. What's the position here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Kordic, Your Honour, as you can see, we do not object to the testimony of this witness; indeed, we think the witness gives significant testimony. But we do object to the summary, and that's the problem. The last sentence is just not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it were to be read out, of course, it would have to be accurate. But at the moment, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But there is an objection, apparently, in relation to Mr. Cerkez. Although Mr. Kovacic isn't here, what is the Prosecution position about this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In relation to number 10, the Cerkez objection is -- I'm sorry. I missed the point, because my form still says "no objection" -- oh, I see, yes, it does. I was just reading it. It's possible that we could delete the Cerkez passages if they are challenged and let the balance go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps you could talk to Mr. Kovacic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Alternatively, we could come to some other compromise on that issue, yes. I'm sorry to be misreading the document; my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 11, the objection seems to be that it concerns events outside the period of the indictment and is irrelevant. Well, again, that's a matter of admissibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I think that's within the province of the Court to decide whether that should be admissible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 12, we don't have Mr. Kovacic's position. There's a query about the credibility. Well, that's a matter, again, which we can weigh or not. But I see, according to the summary, this witness gives some direct evidence about these two, the two accused. Does anyone wish to say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't appear from the objections made that there's necessarily any challenge to the evidence about the accused. In those circumstances, there is no ground for believing there's additional cross-examination required, because the other matters, insofar as they are made out, are matters of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Speaking for Mr. Kordic's Defence, all of this witness's testimony is challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This witness was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, so clearly a significant participant in events. Speaking for myself, this is the sort of witness who I think maybe should be called. Let me just say something to the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 13 is one of the witnesses I think we've deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 13 is deleted, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Likewise, 14. Your Honour, before we move on, which I think we're going to be moving on to 15, I should tell you that so far as number 12 is concerned, our last understanding was that he is probably not willing to cooperate any further with this Tribunal, although he gave evidence in Blaskic, and therefore he may have to be added to another list for an application in another way. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we'll deal with that when we establish the final position of these witnesses. There may be applications for subpoenas, and we'll have to see what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Number 15, no objection on behalf of Mr. Cerkez; objection on Mr. Kordic's part. A substantial portion of closed session testimony has not been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that material was served yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have not had the opportunity to review it, but we'd be more than happy to provide the Trial Chamber with our updated position tomorrow morning, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 16, no objection. Number 17, no objection from Mr. Cerkez. This is the description of an attack on Svinjarevo on the 18th of April; this is then a village witness. Objection is made to the inconsistent testimony and the weight to be attached to the evidence. More significant, again, no closed session testimony received or all the exhibits. Can the Prosecution help with that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can provide those items listed in those two columns of the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you do that today or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would think so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- over the next 24 hours, please. Number 18, this is a witness again about the fighting in the Vitez area. It's a BritBat witness. There is a question about the relevance; again, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber. Also about its probative value; again, for the Trial Chamber. Important videotape evidence, it says, requires direct questioning. Can you assist, Mr. Sayers? Is there anything else you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe the videotape was actually taken in Ahmici on the 16th of April, as the British Battalion units were patrolling not just one part of the village, as has been testified to by several witnesses, but actually all over the village; the lower part, the upper part, all along the road that joins the lower part and the upper part. I think that this witness could throw some light upon the progress of the fighting that actually took place in the village on that day. I would also point out that, as the Trial Chamber obviously knows, it's been difficult for us to determine exactly what happened in Ahmici, and I know that it's been the subject of extensive findings in other cases and discussions in other cases, but I think the final chapter on what actually happened in that village on that day has yet to be written, and it's important for us to be able to conduct some examination of the people who were actually there and who actually saw the fighting. Unless my memory fails me at this point, I do not believe that anybody has actually testified to that in this Trial Chamber to date. So this would be one witness, not necessarily the best witness, but really one witness who could throw some light on that subject. I would also point out, Your Honour, that many of the witnesses testified to the same thing, and there comes a point at which the additional probative value of cumulative testimony is really approaching zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's, I think, again for the Trial Chamber to decide. This videotape, did this witness produce it, or is it a totally separate document, exhibit, which you would like to ask him some questions about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Dredging the recesses of my memory, I think that he did produce it, that the videotape footage was actually shot by him, or soldiers under his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Moving on to number 19, another BritBat witness, what does this witness add? The point is made that it's cumulative. What would he add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have to defer somewhat to Mr. Lopez-Terres on this, but this one we think is -- when we reviewed these again, at the Court's request, and when we eliminated four -- actually, more than four ultimately, there are aspects of this witness's -- it doesn't go just to Ahmici, which everyone is quick to say there's plenty of evidence perhaps, but to other areas of the Vitez municipality and Stari Vitez. Frankly, Your Honour, it's not sufficient for the Defence to say on some of these witnesses that the evidence is just entirely cumulative, because obviously sometimes that varies from village to village. And based on our second review, we felt that this additional testimony was needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Similarly, number 20, and presumably the same arguments apply, 19 and 20. We can see what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to witness number 20, Your Honour, I do recall reading this witness's testimony, and there really isn't anything upon which Major Hunter throws any additional light that hasn't been testified to by many witnesses in this case. It seems that the principal -- at least speculating for the Prosecution's reason why he would be included, the principal reason would be to throw some light upon what happened at Stupni Do, but we've already heard from at least two witnesses who were present at, I think, the security checkpoint that seems to be referred to at the end of this summary. So I don't really think that he adds anything at all, subject to being corrected by the Prosecution, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He may fall into a different category from the witness before, who does, indeed, provide a lot of detail, some of which may not be duplicated elsewhere, and unless either of my learned friends draws my attention to something that's additional, Mr. Sayers' point might be valid, particularly bearing in mind that there's going to be, I hope, another witness on Stupni Do who's coming the week after next and who's going to deal with matters relating to Vares and, to some degree, to Stupni Do in rather more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So for the moment, we can strike that one out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that we could concede that that one could go, yes, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 21, this witness speaks of Mr. Kordic coming to inspect the prisoners. The Defence say they want to cross-examine about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To be specific with respect to this witness, Your Honour, the implication, I think, emerges from the summary that Mr. -- well, it's not clear from the witness's testimony, but it's the Kiseljak barracks that this witness is talking about. I think, as we read his testimony, he implies that Mr. Kordic was seen supposedly in the Kaonik facility, but we contest that. We think that's not correct, and we think the witness was actually detained for a short time in the police station actually in Busovaca, not in the Kaonik barracks. So that's what we would seek to elucidate with this witness on cross-examination, and it has, I suppose, some significance on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
