utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's the narrow issue between the parties, it may be that we can negotiate an excision of the relevant part of the evidence, particularly if, as I believe the position is, this witness may now be an unwilling witness. So perhaps we can arrange to negotiate with that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And with Mr. Kovacic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and then the balance may be admitted, subject to the excision of that or correction of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 22, there seems to be agreement. Number 23, an attack on -- a village witness again, an attack on Gromiljak. A point is taken about the testimony about the number of people having died and said that there is no basis for it. Again, this is a weight point, isn't it, admissibility/weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And again it's a village witness. Number 24, the objection here is, from Mr. Kordic, is that this is an expert and should be subject to the expert procedure. Has the Prosecution got anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we are more concerned to have the value of his evidence on factual findings about destruction of religious properties rather more than to rely on any reliance and dependence on expertise, and it may be possible to negotiate an agreement about that. But I see the objection is very wide-ranging. Perhaps it would be helpful to hear what the full scope of the objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Speaking for Mr. Kordic, Your Honour, we really question the incremental utility of yet more expert testimony in this case on points which seem to be, at least to me, peripheral in a case which is a war crimes case, essentially. He did testify as an expert in Blaskic, I believe, and now the Prosecution says that his factual testimony is all mixed in with the expert testimony. I don't know how you would go about separating one from the other, in all candour. We do point out if he is an expert, then the Rules address how expert testimony is to be put on, should the Court deem it to be necessary, which we do not believe it to be, and we would merely point out that there has been noncompliance with the applicable Rule, 94 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just add to that one or two things. The Chamber has itself, in its Tulica decision, made clear that it's able, with material, to distinguish between conclusions and factual findings. It will remember in relation to the reports that it allowed in on post-mortems and whatever it was that said, "Well, insofar as the report is based on judgement, we will disregard it, we will just look at it for the factual findings," and it may be possible to take the same approach in relation to this. There is, I think, no other expert evidence on this topic that we've presented. The Chamber will recall the line between expertise and non-expertise delineated by the Defence in relation to Mr. Cigar, and it may well be that a great deal of his evidence on that test would fall the factual side of expertise. I'm reminded, I'm sorry, to rise again. According to my friend, his evidence was simply in the form of an UNESCO report rather than as expert testimony. Whether he was formerly categorized as an expert or not, I'm not sure. So it may be another case of the Defence asserting that someone is an expert when, in fact, he gave evidence in fact. We'll have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 25, a detainee in Vitez. No objection from Mr. Sayers. We'll check the position with Mr. Kovacic. Number 26 gives direct evidence apparently about Mr. Kordic. Now, having said what I have about that, what is the Prosecution position about this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there's any expressed challenge to the evidence, which is what she saw of him and how he was portrayed and what her belief was. The objection seems to be, in part, to the summary and relates to something under the cross-examination of Mr. Nobilo that I'm afraid I don't fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The objection apparently is to the cross-examination. That may be a matter which you could discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 27 is another BritBat witness. Again, is that adding anything to what we've already heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only respond again generally. Our list is now the product of two separate reviews, and it was our judgement that there were details on items that were good reasons for including the witness's transcript. In all honesty, I can't stand here and tell you exactly what those details were now, but this list is the product of at least two separate reviews in which we did eliminate some transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 28, what is the objection here, Mr. Sayers? Number 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This witness, Your Honour, testified for about five days relatively early on in the Blaskic case, and a huge quantity of ECMM documents that apparently was not available to the Blaskic Defence has now become available in this case, although obviously not all of them. But nonetheless, the documents that have come available would enable us to test this witness's recollection and version of certain things. I would point out that this witness -- I don't know whether the Court has it in mind, but this witness gave a witness statement that spoke, for example, to the Zenica shelling on the 19th of April, and the chronology of events recited in his statement is substantially at odds with the testimony of others, and we would propose to cross-examine him about that. But this is a witness who pretty much spans the spectrum and gives evidence that's specific to Mr. Kordic as well, and we would like to cross-examine him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although our original intention was to have him dealt with by way of transcript, and if appropriate, he still could be. We have, in fact, listed him as a witness for the last week of the case, in light of the Defence objection, and I believe he's available. I'm not sure. We would take him, I have to say, as shortly as we possibly and sensibly can, but he is currently listed to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 29, no objection as far as Mr. Kordic is concerned. We have yet to hear from Mr. Kovacic. Perhaps, Mr. Nice, it would be helpful if during the adjournment you had a chance to talk to Mr. Kovacic about this to see what remains in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll perhaps meet him here, if I possibly can, about half an hour before we sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 30, objection that it's cumulative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as I can see, this witness adds absolutely nothing to the numerous witnesses who have already testified and Colonel Landry, who apparently is going to testify, who works for the same organization and his testimony covers precisely the same things in the same periods. So it absolutely escapes me, why this testimony would be necessary or what point upon which it is offered to prove. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 31, what's the objection there? You say his evidence is inconsistent with other evidence. You can point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I think that's the sum and substance of our position, and there's no point in beating a dead horse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Number 32, I'm not sure I follow quite what's happening with 32. It's described in the Defence document as "OTP error." Is this still a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. The summary was actually for another witness, I think, Mr. Mladen Veseljak. We have objected because we have not been supplied with closed-session testimony and some exhibits. I believe the Prosecution, some days ago, did supply us with those missing items that were referred to in this document, and accordingly we would like to change the objection to no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We were prepared to delete this one. That's why I'm standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were prepared to delete it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you are prepared to delete it, then let us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And likewise 33, because that topic is going to be covered by someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 34, there's no objection as far as Mr. Kordic is concerned. We need to hear from Mr. Kovacic. Again, it might be helpful if the Prosecution might negotiate and see what the position is there. Number 35 is another BritBat witness. Objection is made about the cumulative nature of that. Again, I take it there's nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just add on that particular item, and again I just caution -- if the Court will allow me just to caution the Court a bit on these because again there may be arguably -- there may be some argument about conceding the ultimate position about cumulative on some items but not entirely. For instance, this is not only about Ahmici but it touches upon Stari Vitez and Donja Veceriska, about both of whom, in the Prosecution's views, there's substantially less evidence in the record currently than on some of the other items. So I would just caution the Court not to throw the cumulative net too broadly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 36, the position seems to be there is now an objection where there wasn't before. The summary refers to some direct evidence against Mr. Kordic. Anything you want to say about that, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I regret to say, Your Honour, I was not the attorney that reviewed the testimony of this witness, and the attorney who did review it is now in the United States, Mr. Stein. But I do recall discussing with him the fact that this witness does give testimony that's specific as to Mr. Kordic, about a television program that supposedly this witness saw the night before. But we -- like many of these recollections of events many, many years ago, there is no videotape of this apparently, and apparently the witness gave inconsistent versions of it on cross-examination from those which she had testified to on direct. Other than that, I can't really -- I'm not in a position to add anything beyond what's stated in our papers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that, the inconsistency goes to weight and it's available to the Defence to argue that the evidence would be valuable on the general topic of what Mr. Kordic said on the television the night before and thereabouts. It's unlikely that there's going to be any difference in her overall position were she to come live. There's no specific challenge to the evidence, and this is really a question of weight, whether the Chamber will be able to be addressed, if so advised, by parties on one side and the other as to the totality of her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 37, I think, is another witness from the villages, using that term loosely. We've got all the arguments except that that closed-session testimony is missing. Again, is that provided, to be provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm informed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm informed by Ms. Verhaag that all the closed-session testimony was provided yesterday, although, of course, they may not have had a chance yet to consider it. There may be some outstanding closed-session exhibits. Can I endorse what Mr. Scott said about the approach to the village witnesses. We haven't yet gone through the exercise with these witnesses of identifying precisely where there's a village that may, for example, be overlooked. Some of the villages are very small, we know that, but they are specified in the indictment and it's obviously important for us to ensure that in the interests of the overall case and, indeed, in the interests of the people living there, that all the individual places which can be identified as being attacked are the subject of appropriate evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 38, was this a witness who you were going to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, this was the one who I was going to call and said I wasn't going to call a week or so ago. He adds to the general picture, but he does give -- and I think he's the only person to give evidence, over at page 19 of the schedule, he's the only person I think to give evidence on the village of Kazagici. It may well be that that is not challenged, and it's for that reason that his evidence would be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, is that a matter which you could discuss?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I see no reason why that should not be discussed, but I do want to draw the Court's attention to the last point on our objections, which is that he testified in Blaskic to a meeting with Mr. Kordic, and that's inconsistent with the witness statement that he gave to the Prosecution's investigators, and it would be that upon which we would request cross-examination. If that can be excised from the transcript, then we may reconsider our position relating to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My recollection of that account of the meeting is that it's not particularly significant one way or the other and probably can be excised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. To be discussed. Number 39, no objection as far as Mr. Kordic is concerned; we have yet to hear -- again, if you could ask Mr. Kovacic, please, about this, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 40, no objection on behalf of Mr. Cerkez. It's another village witness. Comments are made about the reliability of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a matter of weight, and again this relates specifically to the attack on Visnjica and may be important for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Likewise, 41. Number 42, another witness about the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 42, we've, I think, deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 41 doesn't appear to be the subject of any specific outstanding challenge, and inconsistencies are a matter of weight, if there are such inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 42 is deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 43, there's no objection. Number 44?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's an Ahmici-describing witness. I think I probably better defer to the Defence who will explain their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is a potentially important witness relating to what actually happened in Ahmici, Your Honour. This gentleman -- this officer, I believe, was one of the first officers to arrive on the scene at Ahmici, at 11 a.m., on the 16th of April, 1993, while fighting was still going on, and he testifies that the fighting actually increased in intensity during his sojourn in the village. I believe he spent four hours in the village altogether on the 16th -- actually, not altogether. Four hours on his first sojourn, and he actually came back to the village in the evening and assisted with the collection of bodies and piling them up at the Catholic cemetery. So in terms of Ahmici being one of the seminal events in this entire case, it seems that it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber, at least it seems to me, that it would be helpful to have testimony from a direct eyewitness to the events that occurred on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to add, save to say that no further cross-examination seems to have been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that the position is as stated. We do not object to the introduction of this testimony provided it's all introduced, all of the direct examination, all of the cross-examination, and the exhibits to which the witness referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kovacic hasn't made his position known. I would be grateful if the Prosecution would talk to him. I see that seems to be a matter which is capable of resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 46, again, this deals with a series of meetings which are not of central issue in this case. Again, what is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The objection is precisely that, Your Honour, the meetings referred to are not of any importance, we would submit, to any issue in this case. But the principal objection is that there were a number of diplomatic cables that were provided to counsel for General Blaskic which we have not had the opportunity to scrutinize, and so we're not in a position to be able to evaluate whether a fully effective job was done on cross-examination. I will say, knowing counsel that represented General Blaskic, an effective job of cross-examination was probably done. But I would just simply like to verify that for myself by looking at the cables, and I would predict that once we do look at the cables, we will conclude that no additional cross-examination would be necessary and that our objection will be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that point -- and I'm not going to refer to this witness by name because it is a confidential witness, with Rule 70 issues, among others -- I will say, Your Honour, in terms of the diplomatic communications that are referred to, we've made this request to the United States government. They, like many governments, are reluctant to give up sensitive diplomatic communications, especially absent a showing of real need, and I think I have faithfully conveyed the Defence position to the United States government. Their position simply is -- they understand what the Court's practice or what the Court has said about these matters, that they believe that this witness testified before; that they felt that they were fully cooperative with the Tribunal in making this witness available before; that he was fully cross-examined; that these particular communications were made available in a very limited way: they were not exhibits, they were allowed to be reviewed by one Defence counsel at the United States embassy, and they were never copied or disclosed. And when they asked me, Your Honour, frankly, why wasn't the cross-examination full or complete in the Blaskic case, I could give them no good reason, or why an additional disclosure of these sensitive communications could be made when there's no indication it's likely to result in any significant new or additional cross-examination. So they are reluctant, Your Honour, to disclose these sensitive communications, again, when there's been no specific showing whatsoever that it would result in new cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That deals with the first batch of witnesses, all but the evidence of General Blaskic and a photographer. Clearly, General Blaskic is in a different category and will have to be separately considered. The Trial Chamber will consider the position. We would be grateful if counsel would carry out such negotiations as have been suggested and perhaps report back tomorrow, and we'll try and resolve all matters tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, with Mr. Kovacic here this afternoon at half past two and Mr. Scott taking the next witness, it may be possible for he and I to negotiate outside, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps Mr. Sayers too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that there's one other -- apart from Blaskic himself, there's one other witness that's been the subject of a notice, and perhaps Mr. Scott, in a minute, can just tell you what that's about. There's one other witness as well that we've dealt with that's only recently come to light. I think there's an application before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a -- yes. This was a witness you were intending to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a witness that we intend to offer by transcript, Your Honour. It may be most helpful on this particular one if we can just go to private session for a moment, because I think it will be somewhat artificial, perhaps, to talk about it in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the witness is called, I'm in a position to report on discussions with Mr. Kovacic about transcripts, if that's helpful, although it's true to say that we haven't yet reached a concluded position. The position is that we've been able to agree on certain matters, and Mr. Kovacic requires time to consider the others. I don't know if you would rather have a partial update or whether you would rather put it back until whenever he's going to be able to complete his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, rather than have a partial update, it may be convenient to deal with it sometime tomorrow morning, when you will have had slightly more time to finish. Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honour. We're ready to proceed with the next witness, but there is an application for protection. We can do that part in private session, if the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacic, there's no need to remain if you want to go and go on with your transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
